{{unsolved|mathematics|Can every simplex be dissected into a bounded number of orthoschemes?}}
In geometry, it is an unsolved [[conjecture]] of [[Hugo Hadwiger]] that every [[simplex]] can be [[Dissection problem|dissected]] into [[Schläfli orthoscheme|orthoscheme]]s, using a number of orthoschemes bounded by a function of the dimension of the simplex.{{r|bkks}} If true, then more generally every [[convex polytope]] could be dissected into orthoschemes.

==Definitions and statement==
In this context, a simplex in <math>d</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] is the [[convex hull]] of <math>d+1</math> points that do not all lie in a common [[hyperplane]]. For example, a 2-dimensional simplex is just a [[triangle]] (the convex hull of three points in the plane) and a 3-dimensional simplex is a [[tetrahedron]] (the convex of four points in three-dimensional space). The points that form the simplex in this way are called its [[vertex (geometry)|vertices]].

An orthoscheme, also called a path simplex, is a special kind of simplex. In it, the vertices can be connected by a [[path graph|path]], such that every two edges in the path are at right angles to each other. A two-dimensional orthoscheme is a [[right triangle]]. A three-dimensional orthoscheme can be constructed from a [[cube]] by finding a path of three edges of the cube that do not all lie on the same square face, and forming the convex hull of the four vertices on this path.

[[File:Triangulated cube.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Dissection of a cube into six orthoschemes]]
A dissection of a shape <math>S</math> (which may be any [[closed set]] in Euclidean space) is a representation of <math>S</math> as a union of other shapes whose [[Interior (topology)|interiors]] are [[disjoint sets|disjoint from each other]]. That is, intuitively, the shapes in the union do not overlap, although they may share points on their boundaries. For instance, a [[cube]] can be dissected into six three-dimensional orthoschemes. A similar result applies more generally: every [[hypercube]] or [[hyperrectangle]] in <math>d</math> dimensions can be dissected into <math>d!</math> orthoschemes.

Hadwiger's conjecture is that there is a function <math>f</math> such that every <math>d</math>-dimensional simplex can be dissected into at most <math>f(d)</math> orthoschemes. Hadwiger posed this problem in 1956;{{r|hh}} it remains unsolved in general, although special cases for small values of <math>d</math> are known.{{r|bkks}}

==In small dimensions==
[[File:Altezza.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|The altitude from a sharp angle may fail to dissect a triangle, but the altitude from its widest angle always dissects it into two right triangles]]
In two dimensions, every triangle can be dissected into at most two right triangles, by dropping an [[Altitude (triangle)|altitude]] from its widest angle onto its longest edge.{{r|hh}}

In three dimensions, some tetrahedra can be dissected in a similar way, by dropping an altitude perpendicularly from a vertex <math>v</math> to a point <math>p</math> in an opposite face, connecting <math>p</math> perpendicularly to the sides of the face, and using the three-edge perpendicular paths through <math>v</math> and <math>p</math> to a side and then to a vertex of the face.{{r|hh}} However, this does not always work. In particular, there exist tetrahedra for which none of the vertices have altitudes with a foot inside the opposite face.
Using a more complicated construction, {{harvtxt|Lenhard|1960}} proved that every tetrahedron can be dissected into at most 12 orthoschemes.{{r|len}}
{{harvtxt|Böhm|1980}} proved that this is optimal: there exist tetrahedra that cannot be dissected into fewer than 12 orthoschemes.{{r|bohm}} In the same paper, Böhm also generalized Lenhard's result to three-dimensional [[spherical geometry]] and three-dimensional [[hyperbolic geometry]].

In four dimensions, at most 500 orthoschemes are needed.{{r|tschirpke93}} In five dimensions, a finite number of orthoschemes is again needed, roughly bounded as at most 12.5 million. Again, this applies to spherical geometry and hyperbolic geometry as well as to Euclidean geometry.{{r|tschirpke94}}

Hadwiger's conjecture remains unproven for all dimensions greater than five.{{r|bkks}}

==Consequences==
Every [[convex polytope]] may be dissected into simplexes. Therefore, if Hadwiger's conjecture is true, every convex polytope would also have a dissection into orthoschemes.{{r|tschirpke94}}

A related result is that every orthoscheme can itself be dissected into <math>d</math> or <math>d+1</math> smaller orthoschemes.{{r|debrunner|bkk}} Therefore, for simplexes that can be partitioned into orthoschemes, their dissections can have arbitrarily large numbers of orthoschemes.
